summary: Describes Vouch By Reference, a protocol that adds third-party certification to email. Independent parties can vouch for the owner of the domain name tied to received mail, helping receivers decide how much to trust the sender.

plainLanguage.summary: Before trusting a stranger, you might ask a friend who knows them. This note lets trusted outside groups vouch for the sender of an email.

questions: how does vbr certify email senders
how does vbr use dns txt records
what does mc=transaction mean in vbr
subtitle: How a mail sender can name outside certifiers who will vouch for its domain, checked by receivers through a DNS lookup.

tldr.problem: A receiving mail system has little way to know whether independent third parties will vouch for the owner of the domain name on a message.
tldr.mechanism: The sender adds a VBR-Info header field naming a domain, a content type and the certifiers it expects to vouch for it. The receiver verifies the domain with DKIM, DomainKeys, SPF or Sender ID, then queries a trusted certifier's DNS TXT record.
tldr.outcome: A receiver can learn which message types a certifier it trusts will vouch for, for example to adjust spam scores. RFC 5518 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8553.

today: RFC 5518 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8553. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Third-Party Certification for Email
sections.content:
Vouch By Reference (VBR) adds third-party certification to email. Independent parties can certify the owner of a domain name associated with received mail, and VBR can be performed anywhere along the mail path, by any capable receiving module or by end-user software.

It is a two-part protocol. First, a sender affixes VBR information saying which certification services it believes will vouch for its mail. Second, the receiver queries one or more of those services, using the DNS to distribute the certification information.

A recipient that uses vouching results to adjust spam scores places a great deal of operational trust in the vouching service. The RFC therefore advises choosing such services with care, and possibly using more than one to avoid a single point of failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender says which trusted friends can vouch for it. The receiver then asks one of those friends, picked by the receiver, if the sender really is okay.

sections.title: The VBR-Info Header Field
sections.content:
The sender adds a VBR-Info header field with three mandatory elements, in the form VBR-Info: md=<domain>; mc=<type-string>; mv=<certifier-list>;. They are:

  • md=, the accountable domain, with no default;
  • mc=, the type of content in the message;
  • mv=, a colon-separated list of domain names of services the sender expects to vouch for that kind of content.

No element may contain white space. Case does not matter, though lowercase is conventional. Verifiers MUST accept the fields in any order and SHOULD ignore any other fields. A message may carry several VBR-Info fields; it is a trace header field and SHOULD be added at the top of the header. If there are several, verifiers SHOULD check each in turn or in parallel until a satisfactory certifier is found, and all of them MUST have identical mc= values.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is a name tag on the email. It says who the sender is, what kind of mail this is, and which friends will vouch for it.

sections.title: The Validation Process
sections.content:
A receiver follows four steps. It extracts the domain to certify and the type of message content. It verifies that the domain is used legitimately, with one or more of the authentication mechanisms described in the RFC. It picks a vouching service it trusts, either from the sender's list or from its own preferred set. Finally, it queries that service to find out whether it actually vouches for that content type for that domain.

The receiver MUST ignore certifiers it does not trust. Otherwise, a bad actor could add an authority it set up itself, to vouch for itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver checks the name tag is not fake, picks a friend it already trusts, and asks that friend about the sender.

sections.title: The DNS Query
sections.content:
For each service that appears in both the message's list and the receiver's trusted list, the receiver builds a name from three parts: the domain being certified, the literal label _vouch, and the host name of the vouching service. For somebank.example and certifier-a.example, that gives somebank.example._vouch.certifier-a.example. It then queries that name for a DNS TXT record.

The record holds a space-delimited list of the content types the service certifies, in lowercase ASCII, for example transaction list. A certifier has vouched for a message if the list contains either the message's type or all. The label _vouch was chosen because a name containing it cannot be a valid host name, so it cannot overlap one by accident.

Verifiers MUST join multiple character-strings in the TXT record into one before checking the syntax. They MUST then check that the record is lowercase letters separated by spaces, and discard anything else. This defends against misconfigured records and records synthesized from DNS wildcards. A VBR name MUST have only one TXT record. The RFC notes that the lookup is efficient, that certifiers can add and delete client records quickly, and that it benefits from DNS negative caching.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking the friend is like looking up a special line in a phone book. The line lists the kinds of mail that friend will stand behind.

sections.title: Types of Message Content
sections.content:
Three content types are defined, and the RFC admits these semantic definitions can be read in different ways by different people.

  • all: all mail from the sender.
  • list: email sent to multiple recipients where each piece is identical or very similar to the others.
  • transaction: a response to a specific action of the user, or a notice about an event in the user's account at the sender.

The mc= value is self-asserted, and its purpose is auditing. A sender that cannot get anyone to certify its advertising mail but has a certifier for its transactional mail might mislabel the advertising as transactional. The mc= element leaves an audit trail so certifiers can catch this and remove certification.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of mail labels: everything, mass mailings, and notes about your own account. The label lets friends check the sender is not cheating.

sections.title: Getting a Domain Name You Can Trust
sections.content:
VBR needs a domain name for an accountable party, and a strong basis to believe it has not been spoofed. Senders SHOULD use DKIM, and MAY use DomainKeys, SPF or Sender ID.

  • DKIM (RFC 4871): md= MUST match the domain from one of the DKIM-Signature fields, taken from i= if present, otherwise d=. VBR-Info SHOULD be covered by the signature and SHOULD be placed immediately below the DKIM-Signature field.
  • DomainKeys (RFC 4870): md= MUST equal the d= value of the DomainKey-Signature field, with similar SHOULD rules for signing and placement.
  • SPF (RFC 4408): md= MUST equal the domain in the reverse-path of the SMTP MAIL command, and SPF must give a pass result.
  • Sender ID (RFC 4406): md= MUST equal the domain in the Purported Responsible Address, and Sender ID must give a pass result.
sections.plainLanguage: Before asking a friend about a sender, the receiver first checks the sender's name tag is real, using one of several ID-checking methods.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: VBR lets users trust independent third parties to certify the owner of a domain name, and the party validating the mail might act on that trust in ways that affect its system's security. The receiver MUST ignore certifiers it does not trust. Implementations SHOULD limit how many VBR-Info fields they process per message, to protect against a make-work or denial-of-service attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Only listen to friends you picked yourself, and do not spend forever checking a message that lists far too many.
